I’m 78 years old and I’ve been farming these same fields in Quzhou County since I was a teenager. My body isn’t what it used to be, but I still know every inch of my land. I have about 6 mu that my family and I manage. The winter wheat went into the ground last October, same as always, and now it’s waking up with the spring weather. I don’t see any reason to change the wheat-maize double cropping system — that’s what everybody in my village does, and it’s the only way I know to keep food on the table and some cash in my pocket.

For the wheat, I sowed an improved variety called Jimai, the same one I’ve used for three years because it gives stable yields and the grain station pays a fair price for it. The extension technician told me 15 kg of nitrogen per mu is enough, but last year I did about 18 kg and the heads were noticeably fuller, so I’ll stick with 18 kg N per mu this year, plus 6 kg of phosphorus and 5 kg of potassium. I’ll irrigate three times: once at green-up now, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. Water costs money and pumping is getting expensive, but I’d rather pay for the water than lose half my crop to drought. I’ll spray pesticide twice — a herbicide when the weeds start coming up, and a fungicide at heading to prevent rust.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I’ll immediately rotary till the stubble and plant hybrid maize, probably Zhengdan 958. It’s reliable and my neighbor Old Wang gets over 600 kg per mu with it. I’ll put down 16 kg N, 5 kg P, and 4 kg K per mu for the maize. I’ll irrigate twice if the summer is dry, especially at the big flare stage, and spray herbicide once at seedling stage, plus an insecticide if I see borers. I expect about 520 kg/mu from the wheat and 600 kg/mu from the maize if the weather cooperates. I’m not trying anything fancy — at my age, stability is worth more than gambling on a new crop.
